title: HIS-201 Ch. 3 — 2 Names
subject: HIS-201
topic: Chapter 3: Colonization and Conflict in the South

cards.def: Powhatan was the weroance who united the Chesapeake Algonquians into a powerful confederacy and tolerated the English to gain trade goods and weapons against Piedmont rivals.
The Powhatan Confederacy united about thirty Chesapeake villages and some twenty thousand people under Powhatan until English expansion shattered its power.
The Pamunkeys were Powhatan's own people, whose homeland was gradually covered by English tobacco fields as colonization spread.
Pocahontas was Powhatan's favorite daughter, whose marriage to John Rolfe sealed an alliance that briefly eased relations between the Powhatans and the English.
John Smith was a soldier of fortune who briefly imposed order at Jamestown, bullied Indians into supplying food, and wrote influential accounts of Virginia.
John Rolfe was the Jamestown colonist who developed a marketable Virginia tobacco, starting the boom that fed English land hunger and labor demand.
Opechancanough was Powhatan's brother and successor who led great attacks on the tobacco colonists, but English retaliation destroyed the confederacy's power.
The Virginia Company of London was the joint-stock company that founded Jamestown in hopes of profit and governed early Virginia until the king dissolved it.
Jamestown was England's first permanent American settlement, built on Powhatan land, where disease, hunger, and conflict with Indians nearly destroyed the colony.
The House of Burgesses was Virginia's elected assembly, which began the tradition of representative government in England's American colonies.
The Calverts were the Catholic proprietors of Maryland who controlled its land and government and granted religious freedom to all Christians.
Charles II was the English king restored to the throne who began a more consistent colonial policy demanding that colonies enrich England.
Nathaniel Bacon was a wealthy frontier planter who led a rebellion against Governor Berkeley's Indian policy and favoritism, attacking Indians and burning Jamestown.
William Berkeley was Virginia's royal governor whose defensive Indian policy and favors to a small circle of allies angered frontier farmers and provoked Bacon's Rebellion.
John Coode was a Protestant Maryland planter who led a revolt against Calvert proprietary rule, which led England to revoke the Calverts' charter for a time.
The gentry were the wealthy Chesapeake planters who dominated offices, courts, and churches and built their fortunes on enslaved labor.
The Royal African Company was the English company that held a monopoly on the English slave trade until competing merchants were allowed in.
Juan de Oñate was a wealthy Spanish colonizer who founded the colony of New Mexico and crushed Acoma Pueblo's resistance with notorious brutality.
Acoma Pueblo was a fortified mesa-top community whose resistance to Spanish demands brought a siege, mass killing, and enslavement that became a symbol of Spanish cruelty.
The Franciscans were Catholic missionaries who built missions in New Mexico and Florida to convert Indians and persuaded Spain to keep its costly northern colonies.
Santa Fe was the Spanish capital of New Mexico, where soldiers, settlers, and captives lived amid the Pueblo communities that bore colonial demands.
St. Augustine was Spain's lasting fortified settlement in Florida, maintained to protect Spanish treasure fleets from pirates and rival colonies.
Popé was a Tewa religious leader who organized the Pueblo Revolt, the most successful Indian uprising against European rule in North America.
The Florida mission Indians lived in Franciscan missions and allied with Spain until Carolina slave raids devastated their towns and destroyed Spain's inland buffer.
Barbados was England's rich Caribbean sugar colony, whose land shortage sent planters and their slave system to found South Carolina.
Charles Town was South Carolina's political and commercial center, where traders organized the Indian slave trade and shipped out the colony's exports.
The Yamasees were South Carolina's Indian trading partners who, fearing enslavement and betrayal, turned on the colony in a war that nearly destroyed it.
The Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Cherokee confederacies traded and raided for the English and survived by playing rival empires against one another.
James Oglethorpe was the Georgia trustee who planned the colony as a refuge for the worthy poor, with small farms and no slavery.
